newsitem.title: USA: Stocks tumble on interest rate fears.
newsitem.headline: Stocks tumble on interest rate fears.

text.p: Stocks tumbled Monday as Wall Street worried anew about long-term interest rates, which flirted with the key 7 percent mark.
Just after 1 p.m. EST, the Dow Jones industrial average was down 73.26 points, or 1.06 percent, at 6,862.20.
In the broader market, declines beat advances by an 18-5 margin on active New York Stock Exchange volume of 265 million shares.
The Nasdaq composite index fell even more sharply and was off 25.71 points, or 2 percent, at 1,267.26. The American Stock Exchange index lost 5.24 points to 595.23.

Investors were gripped by nervousness about interest rates ahead of the March 25 meeting of Federal Reserve policy-makers, with economists divided over whether the Fed will raise short-term rates in a bid to ward off inflation.
"The stock market is pricing in a hike in short-term interest rates by the Fed," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment strategist at First Albany Corp.

In the bond market, the benchmark 30-year Treasury fell 19/32, or $5.94 on a $1,000 bond, pushing its yield to 6.99 percent from 6.94 percent at Friday's close. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
Analysts said long-term rates near 7 percent were spurring investors to sell stocks and to buy bonds.
Roy Blumberg, chief investment strategist at Josephthal Lyon Ross, said the rise in bond yields was especially nerve-wracking for stock investors with stock prices so high.
"When valuations are this high, it is easy to make people nervous," he said.
Larry Wachtel at Prudential Securities, said that technology stocks were "part of the excess that has to be corrected when we take the market down.
"Intel is a perfect example. It has risen 100 points since its July lows. When investors take profits at the end of a quarter, you take them in the areas of excess.

"These stocks are vulnerable and they have to come down sooner or later. Rates are now against us, and the market doesn't thrive when rates go up," Wachtel said. "If you were a money manager sitting on huge gains like the ones in the techs, what would you do?"
Investment guru, Warren Buffet said in his annual letter to shareholders that he believed most stocks were overvalued.
"Buffet has never been known as great near-term timer of the stock market. He is a great investor, that's his speciality," Blumberg said.

"But what he is saying is something that a lot of money managers have been blocking out of their minds -- that in order for stocks to move higher, things have to go very right," Blumberg said. "If things go wrong, even temporarily, people get concerned."
Advanta Corp. lost 8-15/16 to 31-7/16 after it warned of disappointing quarterly earnings.
